outputs.L1: A method for the computer-aided, thematically grouped visual presentation of electronic raw data sets, comprising the following steps: providing a plurality of electronic raw data sets, wherein each raw data set includes, as a property, at least one time specification or one unique identification characteristic; generating a property vector for each of the raw data sets; creating a property matrix whose rows consist of the property vectors; performing calculations on the property matrix, namely calculating clusters of the data sets, calculating associations between selected data, classifying the data sets, and/or calculating summarizations of data sets; reducing the dimensionality of the calculation results to two dimensions; determining the position of the dimension-reduced calculation results in a two-dimensional result space; generating a three-dimensional result space by adding the time specification or the unique identification characteristic as a third dimension to the aforementioned two-dimensional result space; and generating a visual three-dimensional presentation of the three-dimensional result space using a graphical representation of the raw data sets to be visualized.
outputs.L2: A computer-supported process for visually displaying electronic raw data sets by thematic grouping includes the following operations: multiple electronic raw data sets are made available, each of which includes, as an attribute, at least one time-related value or a distinct identifying feature. For every raw data set, an attribute vector is produced, and these vectors are assembled into an attribute matrix in which the individual vectors form the rows. Computational processing is then applied to the attribute matrix, including one or more of the following: determining clusters among the data sets, identifying relationships between selected data, categorizing the data sets, and calculating summaries of data sets. The resulting computational outputs are reduced to two dimensions, and their locations are established within a two-dimensional result space. A three-dimensional result space is then formed by incorporating the time value or the distinct identifying feature as a third dimension into the two-dimensional result space. outputs.L3:
The method begins by providing a plurality of electronic raw data sets. Each raw data set contains data content to be analyzed and includes at least one item of reference information. This reference information may be a time specification, such as a timestamp, time interval, creation time, or measurement time. Alternatively, or additionally, it may be a unique identification characteristic that allows the respective raw data set to be uniquely distinguished from the other raw data sets.

For each of the electronic raw data sets, a corresponding property vector is generated. The property vector represents selected characteristics, features, attributes, or derived values of the respective raw data set in a structured numerical or categorical form. The individual property vectors are then combined to form a property matrix. In this matrix, each row or column may correspond to one raw data set, while the entries of the matrix represent the properties extracted from the raw data.

One or more computational analyses are then performed on the property matrix. These calculations may include clustering, in which similar raw data sets are grouped together; association analysis, in which relationships or correlations between data sets or their properties are determined; classification, in which data sets are assigned to predefined categories; or summarization, in which the information contained in the raw data sets is condensed into a reduced or aggregated representation. Other statistical, machine-learning, or pattern-recognition methods may also be applied to the property matrix.

The results of these calculations are subsequently reduced to a two-dimensional representation. This reduction may involve dimensionality-reduction techniques, projection methods, mapping algorithms, or other transformation procedures that position the calculation results within a two-dimensional result space. In this result space, the relative positions of the data sets may reflect similarities, differences, classifications, clusters, associations, or other relationships determined during the analysis.

A three-dimensional visual presentation is then generated based on the two-dimensional result space. For this purpose, the time specification or the unique identification characteristic associated with each raw data set is added as a third dimension. The raw data sets are represented graphically in the resulting three-dimensional presentation, for example as points, symbols, icons, surfaces, or other visual elements. This enables a user to visually inspect the analyzed data sets not only according to their calculated relationships in the two-dimensional result space, but also according to their temporal sequence or unique identifying order in the third dimension.
outputs.L4:
A computer-aided method is provided for visually organizing and presenting electronic raw data sets in a structured and interpretable manner. The method begins by receiving or accessing a collection of electronic raw data, which may include documents, records, messages, database entries, images, metadata, or other machine-readable information. From this raw data, a plurality of descriptive properties is identified and extracted. These properties may relate to content, context, frequency, semantic meaning, source, category, time, user association, or any other measurable or derivable characteristic of the data.

For each raw data item, the method generates a corresponding property vector. Each property vector represents the selected characteristics of the respective data item in a form that can be processed mathematically. The property vectors are then combined into a property matrix, in which the raw data items and their associated properties are arranged in a structured format. This matrix serves as the basis for further computational analysis.

The method then applies one or more analytical calculations to the property matrix. These calculations may include clustering methods for identifying groups of similar data items, association methods for detecting relationships between data elements, classification methods for assigning data items to predefined categories, or summarization methods for reducing large volumes of data to meaningful representative information. Through these calculations, thematic or structural relationships within the raw data set are identified.

After the analytical processing, the resulting high-dimensional data representation is reduced to a two-dimensional space. This dimensional reduction allows the relationships between data items to be displayed visually while preserving, as far as possible, relevant similarities, distances, groupings, or thematic associations. The two-dimensional representation may show clusters, categories, topical regions, or other organizational patterns within the data.

To enhance the visualization, the method adds a third dimension. This third dimension may represent time, such as the creation date, modification date, occurrence time, or chronological sequence of the data items. Alternatively, the third dimension may represent a unique identifier or another distinguishing attribute that allows individual data items or groups of data items to be separately tracked and interpreted. By adding this additional dimension, the method produces a three-dimensional visualization of the analyzed data.

The resulting three-dimensional display enables users to view electronic raw data sets in a more organized and meaningful form. Thematically related data items can be grouped together, temporal developments can be observed, and individual records can be distinguished within the overall data structure. As a result, large or complex data sets become easier to explore, interpret, compare, and analyze. The method therefore supports improved understanding of relationships within electronic data and provides a visual aid for navigating information that would otherwise be difficult to assess in raw form.

counterfactuals.output:
Below is a sample patent-style method claim. This is not legal advice, and a patent attorney should tailor the claim to the specific invention and prior art.

**Claim 1.** A computer-implemented method of visually presenting raw data collections, the method comprising:

1. receiving, by one or more processors, a plurality of raw data collections, each raw data collection comprising a dataset having one or more data elements;

2. generating, by the one or more processors, a vector representation for each dataset of the plurality of raw data collections;

3. performing, by the one or more processors, one or more analytical computations on the vector representations, the one or more analytical computations comprising at least one of clustering, association analysis, or classification;

4. reducing, by the one or more processors, outputs of the one or more analytical computations to a two-dimensional coordinate space, thereby generating, for each dataset, a first coordinate and a second coordinate;

5. determining, by the one or more processors, for each dataset, a third coordinate based on at least one of temporal information associated with the dataset or a unique identifier associated with the dataset; and

6. rendering, by a graphical display device, a three-dimensional graphical visualization in which each dataset is represented by a graphical object positioned according to the first coordinate, the second coordinate, and the third coordinate, thereby visually presenting relationships among the plurality of raw data collections.

**Claim 2.** The method of claim 1, wherein generating the vector representation comprises extracting features from structured data, unstructured text, image data, sensor data, log data, transactional data, or combinations thereof.

**Claim 3.** The method of claim 1, wherein reducing the outputs to the two-dimensional coordinate space comprises applying principal component analysis, multidimensional scaling, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding, uniform manifold approximation and projection, or an autoencoder.

**Claim 4.** The method of claim 1, wherein the third coordinate represents time, and wherein the three-dimensional graphical visualization displays evolution of relationships among datasets over time.

**Claim 5.** The method of claim 1, wherein the third coordinate represents a unique dataset identifier, entity identifier, source identifier, or session identifier.

**Claim 6.** The method of claim 1, further comprising visually encoding a classification label, cluster membership, association strength, confidence value, or anomaly score using at least one of color, size, shape, opacity, texture, or animation of the graphical object.

**Claim 7.** The method of claim 1, further comprising receiving user input selecting one of the graphical objects and, in response, displaying metadata or raw data elements associated with the selected dataset.
